steps.title: Ask for your server
steps.text: Tell your AI which machine you want: a server, a PC, a laptop. It hands you one setup link, or the one line to paste on that machine. The line installs {product}, gives the machine its own key, and starts the {term:broker} and its {term:link}, now and after every reboot.

steps.title: Your AI works there
steps.text: The machine shows up online. Your AI runs commands, reads and writes files, and asks on your phone before a step that needs your say. Every call is on the record.

features.title: Everything around the terminal. Security built in.

items.text: Before a step that needs your say, your AI asks: what will change, why, and how to undo it. It reaches your phone as a push, and the AI waits for your answer.
Your AI hands you one link for a new machine, your phone or another AI app. The link needs no sign-in: press one button and paste one line, and your AI follows each step until it is done.
Claude and Codex coordinate on one ticket board: claim work, leave notes, hand off.
Linux servers on x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows PCs. Your AI asks the hub which machines are online and works on any of them.
A Docker image and compose with its own Postgres, claimed from your browser with the code from its log. Or the same hub, hosted at {domain}.
Each machine runs a {term:broker} that owns its jobs and a {term:link} that dials out to the hub. Nothing on the machine listens on the network.
Every call through the hub is a row in an append-only, {term:audit}. A call that cannot be recorded is refused.
Each machine proves its own key every time it connects. Revoke it and its link closes within seconds.

self_host.title: Self-host with one command
self_host.intro: On any Linux box with Docker: name your hub once, then one command brings up the hub, its own Postgres and Caddy for TLS.
terminal: # once: get it and name your hub
facts: Claim it in your browser with the {term:claim-code} from its log: `docker compose logs hub`. {pop:claim|How claiming works}
Postgres has no network at all. The hub reaches it over a Unix socket, so there is no database password to keep.
Caddy gets the certificate for your domain.

On a Debian or Ubuntu server, `install.sh` does all of this and keeps the hub current: it pins the image by its {term:digest}, deploys each new one after a backup, and keeps it only if the hub comes up healthy. The database is backed up nightly too.
GitHub builds the image for x86_64 and ARM64 from every commit on main, with signed build provenance you can check.
self_host.hosted: Rather not run it? Use the same hub hosted at {domain}, free during the alpha: your account there is made the first time your AI connects.

next.title: Where it's going
items: **{product}'s own private mesh.** The link moves onto Iroh: your machines connect directly when they can, through a relay when they can't, and fall back to today's link whenever that fails.
**Secrets and devspaces**, from the same hub.

questions.q: Do I have to sign up?
questions.a: No. On the hosted hub your account is made the first time your AI connects. Add a {term:passkey} on your account page afterwards, so you can sign in from anywhere and nothing is lost with one browser.

questions.q: Does anything on my machine accept connections?
questions.a: No. The machine's link opens one outbound WebSocket to the hub and keeps it. No port opens on the machine, so it works behind any router or firewall.

questions.q: What can my AI do on a machine?
questions.a: Start programs as jobs and read their output; read, write and edit files; list folders; read images; and ask you to approve a step. Each machine decides what may run: only the programs you granted, or anything its own account can.

One row per call: the time, the account, the tool, the machine, the job and the outcome, each row chained to the one before by hash. Not the program's arguments and not its output: output passes through to your AI app, and the broker keeps it on your machine.

questions.q: Which systems can join a hub?
questions.a: Linux on x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows. macOS is coming.
No. There are no analytics or tracking scripts, and the broker and the MCP adapter make no network calls at all: the build refuses HTTP client libraries in them.
Any app that connects to a remote MCP server with OAuth: Claude on the web, desktop and phone, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Grok and others. They all use the same address.
Self-hosting runs on your own hardware, with no limit on calls. The hosted hub is free during its alpha.

claim.title: How claiming works

steps.term: The hub prints a claim link.
steps.text: A hub with no owner prints one to its own log each time it starts. Reading that log takes the server, or the platform its container runs on, so someone who only found the address cannot claim it.

steps.term: Open it where your passkey will live.
steps.text: On your phone or your computer. The code rides after the `#` in the link, which a browser never sends, so it stays out of every request and every log. You can also type the code in.

steps.term: Name the owner and make the passkey.
steps.text: One button does both, and you are signed in as the hub's owner.
It is deleted in the same step that stores your passkey, and from then on the hub refuses every claim.

paragraphs: The code is 120 random bits, and the hub keeps only its SHA-256. It works for a day; restarting the hub prints a new one, and only the newest works. A cancelled passkey prompt is retried with the same code.
claim.source: After that: add your machines from your account, and approve each AI app once with your passkey. The rest is in the [docs](/docs).

mcp.definition: Model Context Protocol: the open standard AI apps use to call tools on other systems. Your hub is one MCP server, at one address, for all of your machines.

passkey.definition: A sign-in key your phone or computer keeps and unlocks with your face, fingerprint or PIN. There is no password to steal, guess or reuse.

broker.definition: The {product} service on each machine. It runs what your AI asks as jobs it owns, under the machine's own {product} account, and keeps their output on the machine.

link.definition: The machine's one connection to your hub: a WebSocket the machine opens outward and keeps. Calls come down it, so the machine opens no port.

audit.definition: Every call is a row, and each row carries a hash of the row before it, so changing or deleting an old row breaks the chain where it happened.

oauth.definition: The standard way an app gets permission to act for you without your password. The app asks the hub, you approve it once, and it gets a token you can end.

digest.definition: The SHA-256 fingerprint of one exact container image. Pinned by digest, the hub runs precisely that build, not whatever a tag points at today.

claim-code.definition: A one-time code a hub with no owner prints to its own log. Reading the log takes the server, so only whoever runs the hub can claim it. It works for a day.

https.definition: The encrypted web address your AI app connects to. Your machines dial out to it, so none of them opens a port.
